title: Sign spinning to cheese rolling: the world's strangest championships
excerpt: From a cheese-chasing hill in Gloucestershire to Darwin's beer-can boats, these sporting contests make no sense, and that's the appeal.
content_html:
Not every champion lifts a trophy in front of a packed stadium. Some win by chasing a wheel of cheese down a hill, others by spinning a cardboard sign faster than anyone else.

Here is a round-up of some of the world's oddest sporting contests, and the people who take them seriously.

Sign spinning

US broadcaster ESPN gave sign spinning a national stage this year on ESPN8: The Ocho, its annual celebration of little-known sports. The channel began as a joke from the 2004 film DodgeBall and marked its 10th anniversary in August with almost 75 hours of coverage.

The 2026 sign spinning champion, Doolan, started practising at 14. Competitors qualify through regional events, and judges mark execution, style and technical skill.

Cheese rolling

The Cooper's Hill cheese-rolling event in Brockworth, Gloucestershire, has been held for at least 200 years and possibly more than 600. Racers chase a wheel of cheese down a slope so steep that most tumble rather than run. This year's races were scheduled for 25 May.

The event draws competitors from well beyond England. In 2025, German YouTuber Tom Kopke defended his title in the men's race, while American Ava Sender Logan won the women's race at her first attempt.

Darwin Beer Can Regatta

Australia's own contender began in 1974. After Cyclone Tracy devastated Darwin, thousands of workers arrived to rebuild the city, and locals began building boats out of the empty cans. The regatta has been held ever since.

Cardboard tube fighting

The Cardboard Tube Fighting League stages bouts in the United States and Australia. Fighters wear flimsy homemade armour and try to break their opponent's cardboard tube while keeping their own intact. Anyone aged five or older can enter.

Extreme ironing

The sport began in Leicester, England, in 1997. Competitors iron clothes in unlikely places, from cliff faces to mountain tops.

Haggis hurling

The man credited with inventing this "ancient" Scottish contest admitted in 2004 that its history was a hoax. People kept hurling anyway, and it remains a fixture at Scottish events.

Why they last

These contests are hard to explain to outsiders. They last because the towns and communities that started them keep turning up every year.
